claims.claim: The Tsimane remained relatively isolated from the larger Bolivian economy until the 1970s.
claims.source: The Tsimane remained relatively isolated from the larger Bolivian economy until the 1970s and still widely practice traditional subsistence (swidden horticulture, hunting, and fishing), which contributes >90% of their calories (Gurven et al., 2017; Kraft et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the study population supported by citations.

claims.claim: Traditional subsistence contributes >90% of Tsimane calories.
claims.source: The Tsimane remained relatively isolated from the larger Bolivian economy until the 1970s and still widely practice traditional subsistence (swidden horticulture, hunting, and fishing), which contributes >90% of their calories (Gurven et al., 2017; Kraft et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on Tsimane subsistence.

claims.claim: Respiratory infections are the leading cause of death at all ages among the Tsimane.
claims.source: In terms of morbidity and mortality, the Tsimane are characterized by high infectious disease burden, with respiratory infections as the leading cause of death at all ages (Gurven et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on Tsimane mortality.

claims.claim: Parasites such as helminths and giardia are highly prevalent among the Tsimane.
claims.source: Additionally, parasites such as helminths and giardia are highly prevalent (Blackwell et al., 2013; see also Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation and reference to data in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The Tsimane have a low incidence of chronic conditions such as hypertension or atherosclerosis.
claims.source: These conditions result in frequent, acute immune responses (Blackwell et al., 2016a) but still a low incidence of chronic conditions such as hypertension or atherosclerosis, due to high levels of physical activity and other protective factors (Gurven et al., 2012; Gurven et al., 2016; Gurven et al., 2009; Kaplan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on Tsimane health.

claims.claim: Wealth varied considerably by age among the Tsimane.
claims.source: Because wealth varied considerably by age (Figure 1A), we used an age-corrected measure of relative wealth that reflects one's wealth relative to this age trajectory (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the relationship between wealth and age.

claims.claim: Mean wealth was generally lowest in Tsimane communities located in the interior forest and those downriver from San Borja.
claims.source: Mean wealth was generally lowest in communities located in the interior forest (Figure 1C, bottom right), which are remote and inaccessible by road for much of the year (due to washed-out bridges); and in those communities downriver from San Borja (Figure 1C, top), which experience frequent flooding and are within or adjacent to a protected bioreserve that limits resource extraction.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C and descriptive analysis.

claims.claim: Mean wealth was higher further from the market town of San Borja among the Tsimane.
claims.source: Somewhat unexpectedly, mean wealth was higher further from the market town of San Borja (correlation between mean wealth and distance to market r = 0.36, df = 38, p=0.02).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: Wealth inequality was generally higher in Tsimane communities closer to the market towns of San Borja and Yucumo.
claims.source: Wealth inequality was generally higher in communities closer to the market towns of San Borja and Yucumo, where Tsimane can sell produce and purchase market goods, though some villages near towns also show low inequality (Figure 1D) (correlation between Gini and distance to market r = –0.38, df = 38, p=0.01).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: For adults, household wealth was associated with lower systolic blood pressure and lower diastolic blood pressure among the Tsimane.
claims.source: Specifically, household wealth was associated with lower systolic blood pressure (β = −0.01, P>0=0.37, Cohen's d = −0.01 [0.02]) and lower diastolic blood pressure (β = −0.04, P>0=0.02, d = −0.05 [0.02]), though both effect sizes were small and only the latter association had high certainty.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study's statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Community mean wealth was strongly and with high certainty associated with lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure among the Tsimane.
claims.source: Community mean wealth was strongly and with high certainty associated with lower systolic (β = −0.29, P>0=0.00, d = −0.34 [0.09]) and diastolic (β = −0.21, P>0=0.01, d = −0.24 [0.11]) blood pressure.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study's statistical analysis.

claims.claim: For Tsimane juveniles, household wealth was moderately associated with lower odds of respiratory illness.
claims.source: For juveniles ≤ 15 years of age (Figure 3; Supplementary file 1n,o), household wealth was weakly associated with lower total morbidity (β = −0.04, P>0=0.06, d = −0.06 [0.04]), and in particular, moderately lower odds of respiratory illness (β = −0.24, P>0<0.01, d = −0.13 [0.05], OR = 0.79).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study's statistical analysis.

claims.claim: For Tsimane adults, greater inequality was strongly associated with a greater likelihood of respiratory illness.
claims.source: Consistent with predictions of worse health with inequality (P2a), greater inequality was weakly associated with higher blood pressure (systolic: β = 0.05, P>0=0.98, d = 0.06 [0.03]; diastolic: β = 0.02, P>0=0.75, d = 0.03 [0.04]), and strongly with a greater likelihood of respiratory illness (β = 0.35, P>0=0.93, d = 0.20 [0.13], OR = 1.36).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study's statistical analysis.

claims.claim: For Tsimane adults, greater household wealth was strongly and with high certainty associated with having more labor partners.
claims.source: Household wealth was strongly and with high certainty associated with having more labor partners (reverse coded β = –0.13, P>0=0.01, d = −0.49 [0.20]), and weakly and uncertainly, with fewer depressive symptoms (β = −0.04, P>0=0.14, d = −0.05 [0.05]), fewer non-social problems (i.e., self-reported concerns over food insecurity, debt, and illness; β = −0.06, P>0=0.12, d = −0.08 [0.07]), and lower urinary cortisol (β = −0.02, P>0=0.27, d = −0.02 [0.04]).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study's statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The only convincing evidence for mediation was found for depression and non-social problems mediating the effect of household wealth on diastolic blood pressure among the Tsimane.
claims.source: The only convincing evidence for mediation was found for depression and non-social problems mediating the effect of household wealth on diastolic blood pressure; specifically, household wealth was negatively associated with diastolic blood pressure (path c) as well as with depression and non-social problems (paths a; see above, Figure 2), and both depression (β = −0.03, P>0=0.20) and non-social problems (β = −0.08, P>0=0.05) were themselves negatively associated with diastolic blood pressure (paths b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study's mediation analysis.

claims.claim: Overall, there was little evidence of psychosocial mediation of wealth-health associations among the Tsimane.
claims.source: Overall, there was little evidence of mediation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study's mediation analysis.

claims.claim: The likelihood of being diagnosed with respiratory illness was predicted to differ greater than threefold (8–28%) between the least and most unequal Tsimane communities.
claims.source: The likelihood of being diagnosed with respiratory illness was predicted to differ greater than threefold, 8–28%, between the least and most unequal communities indicating substantial fitness costs to inequality.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the study's statistical modeling and predictions.

claims.claim: Systolic blood pressure was predicted to increase by 0.32 SD (4.0 mmHg) and diastolic blood pressure by 0.40 SD (3.7 mmHg) in the most unequal compared to the most equal Tsimane communities.
claims.source: While most Tsimane are not hypertensive and do not have heart disease (Gurven et al., 2012; Kaplan et al., 2017), the predicted effects of wealth and inequality on blood pressure were substantial: systolic blood pressure was predicted to increase by 0.32 SD (i.e., 4.0 mmHg) and diastolic blood pressure by 0.40 SD (3.7 mmHg) in the most unequal compared to the most equal communities; conversely, wealth was protective such that the lowest blood pressures were predicted for people in the richest communities (7.4 mmHg systolic and 4.2 mmHg diastolic lower) and the richest households within communities (1.0 mmHg systolic and 3.1 mmHg diastolic lower).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the study's statistical modeling and predictions.

claims.claim: In high-income countries, changes in blood pressure corresponding to those observed in the Tsimane study correspond to as much as a 10% change in the risk of major cardiovascular disease events.
claims.source: In high-income countries, such changes in blood pressure correspond to as much as a 10% change in the risk of major cardiovascular disease events (see Figure 2 in Ettehad et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on blood pressure and cardiovascular disease.

claims.claim: Among the Tsimane, the observed blood pressure changes correspond to as much as 40 years of age-related increases in blood pressure.
claims.source: Among the Tsimane, it corresponds to as much as 40 years of age-related increases in blood pressure (Gurven et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison with cited data on age-related blood pressure changes.

claims.claim: The range of village-level Gini values in the Tsimane study (0.15–0.43) was similar to that of income inequality among high-income countries.
claims.source: In this context, it is also worth noting that while the range of our village-level Gini values (0.15–0.43) was similar to that of income inequality among high-income countries (e.g., Denmark: 0.24; USA: 0.45), it was considerably lower than the range of wealth inequality in these countries (e.g., Japan: 0.55; USA: 0.81 [Nowatzki, 2012]).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison with cited data on inequality in high-income countries.

claims.claim: The range of village-level Gini values in the Tsimane study was considerably lower than the range of wealth inequality in high-income countries.
claims.source: In this context, it is also worth noting that while the range of our village-level Gini values (0.15–0.43) was similar to that of income inequality among high-income countries (e.g., Denmark: 0.24; USA: 0.45), it was considerably lower than the range of wealth inequality in these countries (e.g., Japan: 0.55; USA: 0.81 [Nowatzki, 2012]).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison with cited data on inequality in high-income countries.

claims.claim: At an international scale, as many as 83% of studies find associations between inequality and health.
claims.source: Literature reviews suggest that at an international scale as many as 83% of studies find associations, while in studies of areas the size of neighborhoods, only 45% find associations (Kondo et al., 2012; Pickett and Wilkinson, 2015; Wilkinson and Pickett, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature reviews.

claims.claim: In studies of areas the size of neighborhoods, only 45% find associations between inequality and health.
claims.source: Literature reviews suggest that at an international scale as many as 83% of studies find associations, while in studies of areas the size of neighborhoods, only 45% find associations (Kondo et al., 2012; Pickett and Wilkinson, 2015; Wilkinson and Pickett, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature reviews.

claims.claim: Household wealth may be inconsistently associated with health because it captures several distinct dimensions of socio-economic status with partly orthogonal effects on health.
claims.source: Finally, another explanation for heterogeneous associations is that our measure of household wealth may capture several distinct dimensions of socio-economic status, with partly orthogonal effects on health.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation offered by the authors.

claims.claim: Greater wealth affords more respect and influence within Tsimane communities, which is associated with lower cortisol and better health.
claims.source: On the one hand, greater wealth affords more respect and influence within communities, which is associated with lower cortisol and better health among the Tsimane (von Rueden et al., 2014) and elsewhere (Decker, 2000); this is likely the dimension captured by our subjective status data.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on wealth, status, and health.

claims.claim: Household wealth is accumulated through participation in the market economy, which is associated with greater stress among the Tsimane.
claims.source: On the other hand, household wealth is accumulated through participation in the market economy, which is associated with greater stress – higher cortisol, blood pressure – among the Tsimane (von Rueden et al., 2014) and elsewhere (Dressler, 1999; Konečná and Urlacher, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on market participation and stress.

claims.claim: Conflicts and depression were associated with lower BMI and blood pressure among the Tsimane.
claims.source: Conflicts and depression were associated with lower BMI and blood pressure, perhaps indicating the effects of stress or lack of access to resources (depression is associated with low productivity among the Tsimane; Stieglitz et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study's data analysis and citation.

claims.claim: Depression and non-social problems were associated with worse self-rated health among the Tsimane.
claims.source: Depression and non-social problems were associated with worse self-rated health, again possibly via stress or direct effects of resource availability.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study's data analysis.

claims.claim: A single urinary cortisol measure likely captures overall differences in cortisol excretion but does not capture changes in diurnal cortisol patterns that are typically associated with chronic stress.
claims.source: It is also possible that our measures of psychosocial stress were inadequate, for example, a single urinary cortisol measure likely captures overall differences in cortisol excretion (Yehuda et al., 2003), but does not capture changes in diurnal cortisol patterns that are typically associated with chronic stress (García et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on cortisol measurement.

claims.claim: Objective household wealth correlated significantly, albeit weakly, with subjective status among the Tsimane.
claims.source: Furthermore, household wealth correlated significantly, albeit weakly, with subjective status (Amir et al., 2019; Woolard et al., 2019; r = 0.17, df = 147, p<0.05) and subjective wealth rank (r = 0.29, df = 150, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and citations.

claims.claim: More visible forms of wealth influenced subjective health more than less visible forms of wealth among the Tsimane.
claims.source: Previous work among the Tsimane (Undurraga et al., 2016) has also shown that more visible forms of wealth, such as the household items counted here, influenced subjective health more than less visible forms of wealth, such as the size of cultivated fields.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on the Tsimane.

results.result: Among the Tsimane, greater household wealth was associated with better health outcomes including lower blood pressure, reduced respiratory illness in juveniles, and more labor partners. Community mean wealth was strongly associated with lower blood pressure in adults.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C51, C52, C53, and C55 collectively demonstrate that wealth is associated with beneficial health outcomes. The statistical analyses show significant associations with appropriate effect sizes, though many effects are small. The consistency across multiple health indicators and the use of Bayesian multilevel models with appropriate controls strengthen these findings.

results.result: Greater wealth inequality among the Tsimane was associated with increased respiratory disease and higher blood pressure. The predicted difference in respiratory illness diagnosis between least and most unequal communities was threefold (8-28%), and blood pressure differences were substantial (4.0 mmHg systolic, 3.7 mmHg diastolic).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C54, C58, and C59 provide converging evidence that inequality negatively affects health. The respiratory disease finding is particularly significant given it is the leading cause of mortality in this population. The blood pressure effects, while in a subclinical range for the Tsimane, are substantial and comparable to 40 years of age-related increases.

results.result: Psychosocial factors (depression, social conflicts, cortisol, social support) did not mediate the associations between wealth/inequality and health outcomes among the Tsimane, with only minimal evidence for mediation of the wealth-diastolic blood pressure relationship through depression and non-social problems.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C56, and C57 are supported by formal mediation analyses showing little evidence for psychosocial pathways. The lack of mediation is clearly documented through path analyses, though the authors acknowledge potential limitations in their psychosocial measures (e.g., single cortisol measurement).

results.result: The authors conclude that relative socio-economic position and inequality may affect health across diverse societies, though effects are likely exacerbated in high-income countries due to evolutionary mismatch and chronic disease epidemiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C7 represent broad interpretive conclusions that extend beyond the data. While the Tsimane findings support some hierarchy-health associations, the comparison to high-income countries is largely speculative. The heterogeneous results and lack of psychosocial mediation complicate the interpretation of universality.

results.result: Wealth and inequality varied systematically across Tsimane communities. Wealth varied by age, was lowest in remote interior and flood-prone communities, unexpectedly higher further from market towns, and inequality was higher near market towns.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 describe the distribution of wealth and inequality with supporting statistical analyses and visual evidence (Figure 1). The unexpected finding that wealth was higher further from San Borja is acknowledged and documented with correlation statistics (r=0.36, p=0.02).

results.result: The Tsimane are a population of >16,000 Indigenous Amerindians in lowland Bolivia who practice traditional subsistence contributing >90% of calories, have high infectious disease burden with respiratory infections as the leading cause of death, and low incidence of chronic conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 provide descriptive information about the study population supported by citations to prior work. These characterizations are essential for contextualizing the study but represent background information rather than novel findings.

results.result: The observed blood pressure changes in the Tsimane correspond to substantial health impacts: in high-income countries they would represent a 10% change in cardiovascular disease risk, and among the Tsimane they equal 40 years of age-related blood pressure increases. The Gini range (0.15-0.43) was similar to income inequality in high-income countries but lower than their wealth inequality.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 provide important contextualization of the blood pressure findings through comparisons with cited literature. The comparisons are appropriately qualified and help interpret the clinical/biological significance of the statistical findings.

results.result: The authors propose that household wealth may capture distinct dimensions of socio-economic status with opposing effects: wealth affords respect and influence (associated with better health), but is also accumulated through market participation (associated with greater stress).
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 represent speculative explanations for heterogeneous findings. While supported by citations to prior work, this interpretation is offered as a possible explanation rather than a tested hypothesis. The authors acknowledge this is speculation to explain inconsistent associations.

results.result: Among the Tsimane, conflicts and depression were associated with lower BMI and blood pressure, while depression and non-social problems were associated with worse self-rated health.
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C70 are supported by the study's data analysis. However, the directionality of some associations (lower blood pressure with depression) is unexpected and the authors acknowledge uncertainty about mechanisms. These findings are descriptive associations rather than causal claims.

results.result: The study's measures had limitations: single urinary cortisol may not capture diurnal patterns associated with chronic stress, objective wealth correlated only weakly with subjective status (r=0.17-0.29), and visible wealth forms influenced subjective health more than less visible forms.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 acknowledge methodological limitations supported by citations and correlation analyses. These are important qualifications that appropriately temper interpretation of null findings, particularly regarding psychosocial mediation.

results.result: The introduction establishes that in high-income countries, relative socio-economic position and inequality affect health through psychosocial stress mechanisms, with extensive evidence from human and primate studies showing effects on cortisol, immune function, depression, and various health outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C8-C25 represent established knowledge from prior literature, appropriately cited throughout. These claims provide the theoretical framework and justify the study hypotheses but are not novel findings from this work.

results.result: Prior studies in subsistence societies, including previous Tsimane research, have shown mixed results regarding associations between socio-economic status, inequality, and health, with some evidence that market integration generates stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C40 accurately summarize prior literature on subsistence societies with appropriate citations. The characterization of mixed results is fair and provides important context for the current study's contribution. These are literature review claims rather than novel findings.

results.result: Literature reviews show that 83% of international-scale studies find inequality-health associations, while only 45% of neighborhood-scale studies find such associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C64 and C65 accurately report findings from cited literature reviews. These statistics are used to contextualize the scale at which inequality effects are measured in the current study.
